**Given:** The qubit computational basis and the diagonal states and maps in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-it-finite-dimensional-quantum-relative-entropy]]: $D(A\|B)$ is the natural-log spectral expression under support inclusion and equals $+\infty$ when support inclusion fails.

[F2] [[def-qc-fidelity]]: root fidelity is $F(\rho,\sigma)=\|\sqrt\rho\sqrt\sigma\|_1$.

[F3] [[def-qc-trace-distance]]: trace distance is $d_{\rm tr}(\rho,\sigma)=\frac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1$.

[F4] [[def-qc-trace-norm]]: the trace norm is the sum of the singular values.

[F5] [[def-qc-density-operator]]: a density operator is nonnegative and has trace one.

[F6] [[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]]: positive diagonal operators have the diagonal positive square roots obtained by taking square roots of their eigenvalues.

[F7] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: the natural logarithm is defined on positive reals, is strictly increasing, and obeys the usual logarithm laws.

[F8] [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]]: sine is strictly increasing on $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$.

[F9] [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]: $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ and $\cos(\pi/2)=0$.

[F10] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]]: sine and cosine satisfy their addition formulas, including $\sin(u-v)=\sin u\cos v-\cos u\sin v$ and $\cos(u-v)=\cos u\cos v+\sin u\sin v$.

[F11] [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]: $\sin^2t+\cos^2t=1$ for every real $t$.

[F12] [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]]: $(\sin t)'=\cos t$ and $\cos' t=-\sin t$.

[F13] [[thm-chain-rule]] and [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: the chain and product rules permit two differentiations of the displayed trigonometric identity.

[F14] [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]: differentiability of cosine implies continuity at the endpoint limit used below.

[F15] [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]]: $\pi$ is positive, so the intervals and angles in the Statement have the stated order.



1.1 For $\theta\in[a,\pi/4]$, $\rho_{\sin^2\theta}=\operatorname{diag}(\cos^2\theta,\sin^2\theta)$ is nonnegative and has trace one by [F11], so is a state by [F5]. Since $a>0$ by [F15], [F8] and [F12] make sine positive and strictly increasing on $[a,\pi/4]$; squaring preserves strict order there, so the angle parametrization is injective and $T_a$ is well-defined. Its output angle lies in $[0,\pi/4-a]$, so its output is also a density operator. [given, F5, F8, F11, F12, F15, algebra]

1.2 If a quantum channel agreed with $T_a$ on $\mathcal S_a$, complex-linearity would make its output's $|1\rangle$ diagonal entry affine in $p$, since $\rho_p=(1-p)|0\rangle\langle0|+p|1\rangle\langle1|$. Thus there would be constants $A,B$ with $\sin^2(\theta-a)=A+B\sin^2\theta$ for every $\theta\in[a,\pi/4]$. Differentiating twice on the open interval and using [F10]–[F13] gives $\cos(2\theta-2a)=B\cos(2\theta)$. By [F14], cosine is continuous, so taking $\theta\uparrow\pi/4$ yields $\sin(2a)=0$, because $\cos(\pi/2-2a)=\sin(2a)$ and $\cos(\pi/2)=0$. But $0<2a=\pi/6<\pi/2$ by [F15], so [F8]–[F9] give $\sin(2a)>0$, a contradiction. Hence no quantum channel agrees with $T_a$ on the family. [given, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, F13, F14, F15, algebra]

2.1 For $\theta,\phi\in[a,\pi/4]$, the square roots in [F6] are diagonal with entries $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ and $(\cos\phi,\sin\phi)$. Their product is positive diagonal, so by [F2] and [F4], $$F(\rho_{\sin^2\theta},\rho_{\sin^2\phi})=\cos\theta\cos\phi+\sin\theta\sin\phi=\cos(\theta-\phi).$$ The cosine addition formula [F10] justifies the last equality. Applying $T_a$ subtracts $a$ from both angles, leaving their difference unchanged; root fidelity is therefore preserved for every pair. [given, F2, F4, F6, F10, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For diagonal qubit states, [F3] and [F4] give $d_{\rm tr}(\rho_p,\rho_q)=|p-q|$. Take $\theta\ge\phi$ in $[a,\pi/4]$. The addition formulas and Pythagorean identity [F10]–[F11] give $\sin^2u-\sin^2v=\sin(u+v)\sin(u-v)$. Therefore $$\sin^2\theta-\sin^2\phi=\sin(\theta+\phi)\sin(\theta-\phi),$$ $$\sin^2(\theta-a)-\sin^2(\phi-a)=\sin(\theta+\phi-2a)\sin(\theta-\phi).$$ Here $0\le\theta+\phi-2a\le\theta+\phi\le\pi/2$, so [F8]–[F12] make the first sine factor in the second line no larger than the corresponding nonnegative factor in the first line; the other factor is the same and nonnegative. Thus the output coordinate difference is at most the input difference, proving trace-distance contraction for every pair. [given, F3, F4, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 Take $\theta=\pi/4$ and $\phi=a$. By strict increase of sine from $\sin0=0$ to $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ in [F8], [F9], and [F12], every angle strictly between zero and $\pi/2$ gives $0<\sin^2\theta<1$; thus both input diagonal states have full support and their relative entropy is finite by [F1] and [F7], since the positive spectral entries have finite natural logarithms. The outputs are $\rho_{\sin^2(\pi/4-a)}$ and $\rho_0=|0\rangle\langle0|$. Since $0<\pi/4-a<\pi/2$ by [F15], the first output has full support, while the second has one-dimensional support; support inclusion fails and [F1] gives output divergence $+\infty$. [given, F1, F7, F8, F9, F12, F15, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Independently, the root fidelity of $|0\rangle\langle0|$ and $|+\rangle\langle+|$ is $1/\sqrt2$: the product of their positive square roots is $(1/\sqrt2)|0\rangle\langle+|$, whose only nonzero singular value is $1/\sqrt2$. Their difference is $\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}$, whose square is $I/2$, so both singular values are $1/\sqrt2$ and [F3]–[F4] give trace distance $1/\sqrt2$. The first support is not contained in the second, so [F1] gives infinite relative entropy. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A control qubit with basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, the target space
$\mathbb C$, and a control-first controlled-unitary convention.

[F1] The phase-insensitive projective class identifies $I$ and $-I$ on the
one-dimensional target. [[def-qc-tqc-projective-gate-and-metric]]

[F2] A controlled global phase becomes a relative control phase and is
observable by a two-outcome measurement.
[[thm-qc-controlled-global-phase-is-relative-phase]]



**Given:** The target starts in its unique unit vector, the control starts in
$|+\rangle=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$, and the measurement is in the
$\{|+\rangle,|-\rangle\}$ basis.

1.1 Uncontrolled on $\mathbb C$, the gates $I$ and $-I$ differ by the scalar $-1$, so they have the same projective class by [F1]. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The controlled $I$ is the identity, so it leaves the control in $|+\rangle$ and the $+$ outcome has probability $1$. The controlled $-I$ is $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ on the control; it maps $|+\rangle$ to $|-\rangle$, so the same outcome has probability $0$. Thus the controlled outcome laws differ, refuting the statement. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The Hopf counit representation, its direct sum on a two-dimensional space, and the one-root Bethe-vector notation from [[lem-yangian-gl2-one-root-bethe-cancellation]].

[F1] [[prop-yangian-gl-n-rtt-hopf-structure]]: $\epsilon(t_{ij}(u))=\delta_{ij}$ defines the counit representation.

[F2] [[lem-yangian-gl2-one-root-bethe-cancellation]]: the one-root condition is $a(v)=d(v)$, and its cancellation theorem assumes the associated Bethe vector is nonzero to conclude it is an eigenvector.



1.1 Let $\mathcal H=\mathbb C e_0\oplus\mathbb C e_1$ be the direct sum of two counit representations and set $\Omega=e_0$. Applying the counit on each summand gives $t_{ij}(u)=\delta_{ij}I_{\mathcal H}$, hence $A=D=I$ and $B=C=0$. Thus the pseudovacuum conditions hold with $a(u)=d(u)=1$, and the one-root equation in [F2] holds for every $v$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 For every $k\ge1$ and parameters $v_1,\ldots,v_k$, the rightmost $B(v_k)$ sends $\Omega$ to zero, so $B(v_1)\cdots B(v_k)\Omega=0$. The empty product is $e_0$. Hence all Bethe vectors from this pseudovacuum span $\mathbb C e_0$, a proper subspace because $e_1$ is linearly independent from $e_0$. Thus the one-root equation by itself does not guarantee completeness. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The finite-dimensional fusion space $V$, the computational space
$\mathcal C$, and an isometry $J:\mathcal C\to V$.

[F1] An isometry satisfies $J^*J=I_{\mathcal C}$.
[[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]]

[F2] The adjoint satisfies $(AB)^*=B^*A^*$ and $(J^*)^*=J$.
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]





1.1 By [F2], $P^*=(JJ^*)^*=(J^*)^*J^*=JJ^*=P$. Also $P^2=JJ^*JJ^*=J(J^*J)J^*=JI_{\mathcal C}J^*=P$ by [F1]. Hence $P$ is an orthogonal projection. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 For every $u\in\mathcal C$, $P(Ju)=JJ^*Ju=Ju$ by [F1], so $J\mathcal C\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P$. Conversely $Pv=J(J^*v)$ lies in $J\mathcal C$ for every $v\in V$, so $\operatorname{ran}P\subseteq J\mathcal C$. Therefore $\operatorname{ran}P=J\mathcal C$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A Majorana system, a fixed parity sector, and the interface
hypotheses in the Definition.

[F1] In the three-$\sigma$, total-$\sigma$ Ising sector, the supplier gives
$R_1=e^{-i\pi/8}$ and $R_\psi=e^{3i\pi/8}$, hence
$R_\psi/R_1=i$. [[ex-qc-tqc-ising-data]]



1.1 Let $A_j=i\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}$. The Majorana relations give $A_j^*=A_j$ and $A_j^2=I$. Therefore $Q_1(j)=(I-A_j)/2$ and $Q_\psi(j)=(I+A_j)/2$ are self-adjoint idempotents, $Q_1(j)Q_\psi(j)=0$, and $Q_1(j)+Q_\psi(j)=I$. They are the orthogonal complementary pair-channel projections stipulated by the interface. [given, algebra]

2.1 Since $(\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1})^2=-I$, expansion of the exponential gives $U_j=2^{-1/2}(I-\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1})$. Its restrictions to $\operatorname{ran}Q_1(j)$ and $\operatorname{ran}Q_\psi(j)$ are respectively $e^{-i\pi/4}I$ and $e^{i\pi/4}I$. Using the phase ratio in [F1] as imposed for every generator by the interface, the channel exchange equals $$R_1Q_1(j)+R_\psi Q_\psi(j)=R_1e^{i\pi/4}U_j.$$ Thus it differs from $U_j$ by one common scalar. [given, F1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The displayed $P,Q$ and the definitions of f-, KL-, and Rényi
divergence below.

[F1] [[def-finite-probability-vector]]: a finite probability vector has
nonnegative coordinates summing to one.

[F2] [[def-finite-kullback-leibler-divergence]]: $D(P\|Q)=
\sum_{x:p_x>0}p_x\log(p_x/q_x)$ with natural logarithms.

[F3] [[def-finite-renyi-divergence]]: for $\alpha\ne1$,
$D_\alpha(P\|Q)=\log S_\alpha(P,Q)/(\alpha-1)$ with the support conventions
stated in its Definition.

[F4] [[def-finite-f-divergence]]: for $f(t)=\frac12|t-1|$, the
f-divergence uses the coordinate terms $q_xf(p_x/q_x)$.



**Given:** $P=(3/4,1/4)$ and $Q=(1/4,3/4)$.

1.1 By [F2], $D(P\|Q)=\frac34\log3+\frac14\log(1/3) =\frac12\log3$. The direction is $P$ to $Q$; reversing the vectors gives the same value here by symmetry. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For order $1/2$, each affinity term is $\sqrt{p_xq_x}$, so $S_{1/2}=2\sqrt{3/16}=\sqrt3/2$ by [F3]. Therefore $D_{1/2}=-2\log(\sqrt3/2)=\log(4/3)$. [F3, algebra]

1.3 For order $2$, [F3] gives $S_2=(9/16)/(1/4)+(1/16)/(3/4)=9/4+1/12=7/3$, so $D_2=\log(7/3)$. [F3, algebra]

2.1 The generator in [F4] gives $D_f(P\|Q)=\frac12\sum_x|p_x-q_x| =\frac12(1/2+1/2)=1/2$. [F1, F4, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The displayed $P,Q$, the total-variation generator
$f(t)=\frac12|t-1|$, and the KL and Rényi conventions.

[F1] [[def-finite-probability-vector]]: coordinates may be zero, and
$\operatorname{supp}P=\{x:p_x>0\}$.

[F2] [[def-finite-f-divergence]]: a coordinate with $q_x>0=p_x$
contributes $q_xf(0)$, while one with $p_x>0=q_x$ contributes
$p_xf_\infty$.

[F3] [[def-finite-kullback-leibler-divergence]]: any coordinate with
$p_x>0=q_x$ makes $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$; zero $P$-mass contributes zero.

[F4] [[def-finite-renyi-divergence]]: below order one a $p_x>0=q_x$
coordinate contributes zero to the affinity; above order one it makes the
affinity infinite.



**Given:** $P=(1,0)$ and $Q=(0,1)$ on $\{a,b\}$.

1.1 For the total-variation generator, $f(0)=1/2$ and $f_\infty=1/2$. The coordinate $a$ contributes $p_af_\infty=1/2$ by [F2], and coordinate $b$ contributes $q_bf(0)=1/2$. Thus $D_f(P\|Q)=1$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Since $p_a=1>0=q_a$, [F3] gives $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. This records the singular direction; $D(Q\|P)$ is also infinite by the same support calculation with $a,b$ exchanged. [F3, algebra]

2.1 If $0<\alpha<1$, the only coordinate with $q_x>0$ is $b$, where $p_b=0$, so $S_\alpha(P,Q)=0$ and $D_\alpha(P\|Q)=+\infty$ by [F4] and the definition. If $\alpha>1$, coordinate $a$ gives infinite affinity by [F4]. At $\alpha=1$, KL is infinite by step 1.2. [F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The rank-one Coxeter system $W=S_2$, the universal Hecke algebra over its Laurent parameter ring, and the specializations $q=i$, $q=1$, and $q=-1$ over $\mathbb C$.

[F1] [[def-hh-universal-coxeter-hecke-parameters-and-presentation]]: the rank-one quadratic relation is $(T-v)(T+v^{-1})=0$ for a unit parameter $v$.

[F2] [[thm-hh-generic-coxeter-hecke-standard-basis]]: arbitrary scalar extension presents the specialized Hecke algebra by the images of the same quadratic and braid relations, with no flatness assumption.

[A1] $i^2=-1$, so $i^{-1}=-i$ and $i$ is a unit in $\mathbb C$.

[A2] The values $1$ and $-1$ are units in $\mathbb C$ and each has square $1$.



1.1 For any unit $q$, expanding [F1] and putting $S=qT$ gives $S^2=(q^2-1)S+q^2$, equivalently $(S-q^2)(S+1)=0$; thus the multiplicative source parameter is $\xi=q^2$, while all calculations below keep the local $T$ generator. Now set $q=i$. Then [F1] gives $(T-i)(T+i^{-1})=(T-i)^2=0$, and [F2] identifies this as the complete specialized presentation. With $\epsilon=T-i$, translation $T=\epsilon+i$ gives mutually inverse homomorphisms between $H_2(i)$ and $\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$. Every class has a unique form $a+b\epsilon$: terms of degree at least two vanish, and a polynomial of degree at most one lying in $(\epsilon^2)$ has both coefficients zero. Hence the algebra has basis $1,\epsilon$ and $\epsilon$ is nonzero. [given, F1, F2, A1, algebra, construct]

1.2 For $q=1$ and $q=-1$, [F1] gives the same relation $T^2-1=0$, using [F2] for the specialization. The elements $e_+=(1+T)/2$ and $e_-=(1-T)/2$ are orthogonal idempotents with sum $1$. The classes $1,T$ are linearly independent because no nonzero polynomial of degree at most one is divisible by $T^2-1$, so $e_+$ and $e_-$ are nonzero and form a basis. Thus $H_2(q)=\mathbb C e_+\oplus\mathbb C e_-$, and each one-dimensional left ideal is simple. The regular module is semisimple. [given, F1, F2, A2, algebra, construct]

2.1 The left ideal $\epsilon H_2(i)$ is one-dimensional, nonzero and proper by step 1.1, so the left regular module is not simple. If it were a direct sum of simple left ideals, its dimension two would force it to be a sum of two one-dimensional simple modules. On any one-dimensional module, left multiplication by $\epsilon$ is a scalar $\lambda$ satisfying $\lambda^2=0$, hence $\lambda=0$. It would then annihilate both summands and therefore all of $H_2(i)$, contradicting $\epsilon\cdot1=\epsilon\ne0$. Thus the regular module is not semisimple. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Steps 2.1 and 1.2 establish the two different specialization outcomes under the stated normalized relation. They make no claim about higher ranks, centralizers, positive characteristic, or every root of unity. No choice principle is used: every basis, idempotent, and module complement calculation is explicit and finite. [step 2.1, step 1.2, given] ∎

**Given:** The matrices $R(u)$ and $\check R(u)$ of [[def-hh-rational-spectral-r-matrix]], the identities of [[lem-hh-rational-spectral-r-matrix-satisfies-yang-baxter]], and the braid-group representation interface.

[F1] [[def-hh-rational-spectral-r-matrix]]: $R(u)=uI+iP$ and $\check R(u)=PR(u)$.

[F2] [[lem-hh-rational-spectral-r-matrix-satisfies-yang-baxter]]: for all $x,y,z\in\mathbb C$, both the un-checked and checked spectral equations hold with parameters $x-y$, $x-z$, and $y-z$.

[F3] [[def-yang-baxter-operator-on-an-object]]: a Yang-Baxter operator is an invertible endomorphism satisfying the braid-form equation; invertibility is part of the definition.

[F4] [[thm-a-yang-baxter-operator-gives-braid-group-representations]]: an invertible Yang-Baxter operator gives a homomorphism from each Artin braid group B_n into the automorphism group of the corresponding tensor power.



1.1 The flip $P$ has eigenvalue $1$ on the three-dimensional symmetric subspace, with basis $e_1\otimes e_1$, $e_1\otimes e_2+e_2\otimes e_1$, $e_2\otimes e_2$, and eigenvalue $-1$ on the one-dimensional antisymmetric subspace spanned by $e_1\otimes e_2-e_2\otimes e_1$. Therefore $R(u)=uI+iP$ has eigenvalues $u+i$ and $u-i$ on these two subspaces, while $\check R(u)=uP+iI$ has eigenvalues $u+i$ and $i-u$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 At $u=i$, $R(u)$ vanishes on the antisymmetric line and has rank three; at $u=-i$, it vanishes on the symmetric subspace and has rank one. Thus both $R(u)$ and $\check R(u)$ are invertible exactly away from $u=i$ and $u=-i$. At $u=0$, $R(0)=iP$ and $\check R(0)=iI$ are invertible. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Set $x=i$, $y=0$, $z=0$. Then the checked identity in [F2] has the factors $\check R_1(i)$, $\check R_2(i)$, and $\check R_1(0)$, and both $\check R_1(i)$ and $\check R_2(i)$ are singular by step 2.1. Thus these maps cannot be images of braid-group generators in an automorphism group: the required invertibility in [F3] fails. [given, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 At $u=0$ the checked operator is $iI$. Its local operators on every tensor power are scalar $iI$ and satisfy the Artin braid and distant-commutativity relations; they are invertible because $i$ is nonzero. Thus the assignment $\sigma_j\mapsto iI$ does define a braid-group representation, consistent with [F4]. [given, F1, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The fixed Fibonacci fusion rule, the pair and triple fusion trees,
the exact finite-field certificates, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

[F1] The normalized B6 image in $U(5)$ has closure containing $SU(5)$, and
the image in $U(8)$ has closure containing $SU(8)$.
[[thm-qc-tqc-b6-su5-density]] [[thm-qc-tqc-b6-su8-density]]

[F2] The simultaneous B6 closure contains $SU(5)\times SU(8)$.
[[lem-qc-tqc-b6-joint-su5-su8-density]]

[F3] Per-gate full-space errors add; exact logical-block equality for an
ambient unitary forces zero leakage.
[[lem-qc-tqc-leakage-logical-error-accumulation]]
[[lem-qc-tqc-zero-logical-error-forces-zero-leakage]]

[F4] Reduction of coefficients through the stated $\mathbb F_{31}$
specialization sends a zero algebraic determinant to zero.
[[lem-qc-tqc-fibonacci-coefficient-ring-specialization]]

[F5] Three-Fibonacci-anyon braid generators are dense in $PU(2)$ under
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.
[[thm-qc-tqc-fibonacci-single-qubit-density]]

[F6] The six-anyon triple code has dimension $4$ in both total-charge blocks;
in total charge $1$, the ambient dimension is $5$.
[[def-qc-tqc-six-anyon-encoded-subspace]]

[F7] Every admissible fusion tree has its orthonormal path basis, and a
unitary associator composite changes between the pair, triple, and
left-associated trees.
[[def-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-basis]]
[[lem-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-dimension]]
[[def-qc-tqc-unitary-fusion-category]]
[[thm-qc-tqc-gauge-covariance]]

[F8] A full-space approximation by $\delta$ to a code-preserving unitary
target bounds both logical block error and leakage by $\delta$.
[[thm-qc-tqc-block-approximation-error]]

[A1] Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. [[def-countable-choice]]

[A2] Use the Fibonacci fusion rules and the triple-code path convention
stated in [[def-qc-tqc-six-anyon-encoded-subspace]]. The pair-charge code
below is a distinct subspace in the same total-charge block; no equality of
the two code projectors is assumed.



1.1 In the pairwise tree $T_p=(((\tau_1\otimes\tau_2)\otimes(\tau_3\otimes\tau_4)) \otimes(\tau_5\otimes\tau_6))$, let $q_i\in\{0,1\}$ label the charge $1$ or $\tau$ of pair $(2i-1,2i)$, respectively. Fusion to total charge $1$ allows exactly the strings $$000,\quad011,\quad101,\quad110,\quad111.$$ For $000$, the intermediate charge after the first two pair outputs is $0$. For $011,101,110,111$, it is uniquely $1,1,0,1$, respectively; each then fuses with the last pair output to total charge $1$. A string with exactly one $1$ has total charge $\tau$ and is inadmissible. Thus the four even strings span a four-dimensional pair-charge code $\mathcal D_1$, and the all-$\tau$ string $111$ spans its one-dimensional complement. Fix a unitary associator composite from $T_p$ to the left-associated B6 tree. The triple code $\mathcal C_1$ in [F6] is transported to that same tree by its own fixed associator composite. Both are four-dimensional subspaces of the five-dimensional total-charge-$1$ fusion space. The argument below treats them as independent code choices and makes no projector-equality claim. [A2, F6, F7, construct, algebra]

1.2 Let $\mathcal K$ be any four-dimensional subspace of the five-dimensional total-charge-$1$ fusion space, including either $\mathcal D_1$ or $\mathcal C_1$, and let $U\in U(\mathcal K)$. Its orthogonal complement is one-dimensional. Define $T=U\oplus(\det U)^{-1}$ on $\mathcal K\oplus\mathcal K^\perp$; this is unitary with determinant one, so $T\in SU(5)$. By [F1], every operator-norm neighborhood of $T$ contains a normalized B6 word. Applying [F8] to a word within $\delta$ of $T$ gives logical block error and leakage at most $\delta$ for the selected code. Therefore the pair-charge and triple codes each admit the same density guarantee without identifying their subspaces. [F1, F6, F8, choose]

1.3 The five-dimensional certificate runs research/scaffold-audit-2026-10-16/topological-quantum-computing/b6-lie-rank-certificate.py and returns the exact minor determinant $17$ in $\mathbb F_{31}$. The eight-dimensional deterministic selection runs research/scaffold-audit-2026-10-16/topological-quantum-computing/b6-su8-lie-rank-certificate.py and returns determinant $22$. Both scripts use integer arithmetic only; [F4] proves that these nonzero reductions imply nonzero exact complex determinants. [F1, F2, F4, algebra]

1.4 Let $G>0$ be the number of ideal gates and choose $\delta_j=\epsilon/G$ for $1\le j\le G$. Then $\sum_j\delta_j=\epsilon$. By [F2], each adjacent two-qubit target has a joint braid approximation with tolerance $\delta_j$; the one-qubit targets use the dense three-anyon representation [F5]. [F2, F5, A1, choose]

2.1 Applying [F3] to the physical and ideal gate products gives total logical block error and leakage at most $\sum_j\delta_j=\epsilon$. For a concrete distinction between these measurements, take $V=\mathbb C^2$, code $\mathbb C e_0$, target $U=1$, and $$W_\theta=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix},\qquad0<\theta<\pi/2.$$ The compressed block is $\cos\theta$, so its logical error is $1-\cos\theta$, while the leakage amplitude is $\sin\theta$. It has the correct one-dimensional logical direction with reduced amplitude, not an exactly correct block. Conversely, exact block equality forces zero leakage by [F3]. [F3, A1, step 1.4, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The displayed fixed Ising fusion sector, its ordered channel basis,
and the Pauli matrices $X,Y,Z$.

[F1] The Pauli matrices are
$X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$,
$Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$,
$Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$.
[[def-qc-pauli-matrices]]

1.1 Fix $c>0$ and let $u=c/2$, $a=3c/4$, $b=5c/4$, and $v=3c/2$. For $r<s$, write $m(r,s)=(f(s)-f(r))/(s-r)$. If $a\le x<y\le b$, convexity at $a$ between $u,x$, at $x$ between $u,y$, at $y$ between $x,v$, and at $b$ between $y,v$ gives $m(u,a)\le m(u,x)\le m(x,y)\le m(y,v)\le m(b,v)$ by rearranging the four two-point inequalities in [F1]. All these endpoint slopes are finite. Thus with $M=\max\{|m(u,a)|,|m(b,v)|\}$, one has $|f(y)-f(x)|\le M|y-x|$ for $x,y\in[a,b]$, including $x=y$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Fix $a=1/2$ and set $n(x)=(f(a)-f(x))/(a-x)$ for $0<x<a$. If $0<x<y<a$, then $y$ is a convex combination of $x$ and $a$; [F1] gives $f(y)\le\frac{a-y}{a-x}f(x)+\frac{y-x}{a-x}f(a)$. Rearranging yields $n(x)\le n(y)$. Also $a$ is a convex combination of $x$ and $1$, so another application of [F1] gives $n(x)\le(f(1)-f(a))/(1-a)$, a finite upper bound. Therefore $L:=\inf_{0<x<a}n(x)$ is either real or $-\infty$; the infimum property from [F2] gives $n(x)\to L$ as $x\downarrow0$ (if $L$ is finite, approximate it within any $\varepsilon>0$; if $L=-\infty$, use any real lower target). Since $f(x)=f(a)-(a-x)n(x)$, its limit is $f(a)-aL$ if $L$ is finite and $+\infty$ if $L=-\infty$. Thus $f(0)$ exists and is not $-\infty$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $\delta=\min\{c/4,\varepsilon/(M+1)\}$. If $|x-c|<\delta$, then $x,c\in[a,b]$, and step 1.1 gives $|f(x)-f(c)|\le M|x-c|<\varepsilon$. This is continuity at the arbitrary $c>0$, so $f$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$. [step 1.1, given, choose, algebra]

3.1 For $t>1$, put $r(t)=f(t)/(t-1)$. If $1<s<t$, then $s$ is a convex combination of $1$ and $t$. By [F1] and $f(1)=0$, this gives $r(s)\le r(t)$. Hence $r$ is nondecreasing on $(1,\infty)$ and bounded below on $[2,\infty)$ by the finite value $r(2)$. By the supremum property in [F2], its limit is the real supremum $R$ if it is bounded above, and is $+\infty$ otherwise: for finite $R$, values eventually lie between $R-\varepsilon$ and $R$; when unbounded, they eventually exceed any prescribed real number. Since $f(t)/t=((t-1)/t)r(t)$ and $(t-1)/t\to1$, this quotient tends to $R$ if $R$ is finite; if $R=+\infty$, the factor is at least $1/2$ for $t\ge2$ and the quotient tends to $+\infty$. Thus $f_\infty$ exists and is not $-\infty$. [F1, F2, given, algebra] ∎
